analysis.one_liner: Loosens endangered species rules to send more California delta water to farm irrigation districts.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced with zero cosponsors, it got one hearing in September 2014 and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have overridden parts of the Endangered Species Act as they apply to the two big federal and state water projects that pump water out of the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta. It would have removed specific limits on winter and spring pumping designed to protect the delta smelt and salmon runs, barred California from enforcing any stricter rules, and required fish hatcheries and habitat restoration as substitutes. It would have expired in March 2020. It never advanced past its committee.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main gainers would be the agricultural water contractors — irrigation districts and large growers on the west side and south end of the San Joaquin Valley — who buy water delivered through the Central Valley Project and the State Water Project. More pumping means fuller deliveries, less fallowed farmland, and steadier jobs in valley farm towns [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: San Joaquin Valley irrigation districts and growers

how_it_helps.text: It would have declared the Endangered Species Act satisfied for the 2008 and 2009 biological opinions governing project operations, so long as the existing 'reasonable and prudent alternatives' were implemented and specific new pumping floors were met [S2][S3].

It would have barred the wildlife agencies from restricting Old and Middle River flows beyond -5,000 cfs between December and June, blocked spring pumping cutbacks at the Jones and Banks plants, and relaxed the fall salinity standard — the three main restrictions that reduce water deliveries [S2][S3].
It would have required hatchery and habitat programs for delta smelt and other at-risk fish, plus ecosystem restoration and fish passage projects, as the offset for loosened pumping limits [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The costs would fall on the Delta ecosystem and the people who depend on it: endangered delta smelt and salmon runs would lose the specific flow and pumping protections in the biological opinions, and the commercial and recreational fishing economy built on salmon would bear the risk. Californians would also lose the ability to enforce stricter state protections, since the bill preempts any state rule more restrictive than its own [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Delta fish, the salmon fishing economy, and state water rules

drawbacks.text: It would have stripped out the concrete flow and pumping limits that federal biologists set in 2008 and 2009 to keep delta smelt and salmon from being pushed through the pumps, replacing them mainly with hatchery and habitat programs that the bill does not fund [S2][S3].

It would have preempted California law, barring the state from imposing any restriction on project operations stricter than the federal ones — overriding the state's own authority over its water [S2][S3].
The fish-protection side of the bill is a set of directives with no money attached, while the water-delivery side is binding; an honest supporter would concede the trade is not even-handed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's case was real: federal pumping restrictions contributed to fallowed farmland, high unemployment in valley towns, and growing reliance on over-drafted groundwater, all detailed in its own findings [S3]. But the remedy was one-sided — it removed enforceable protections for fish, substituted unfunded restoration directives, and preempted the state's authority, with the whole scheme expiring in 2020 rather than settling the underlying conflict [S2]. As designed, the water gains went to a concentrated set of contractors while the ecological risk was spread to the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, which held a hearing in September 2014 but never advanced it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Jim Costa, a Democrat from California's Central Valley, introduced the bill on May 9, 2013, and no other member signed on as a cosponsor [S1][S4][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the day it was introduced [S5].
The committee held a hearing on September 9, 2014, but never reported the bill or scheduled a vote, and it expired with the 113th Congress [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The delta's fish and the coastal fishing communities that depend on salmon runs kept existing Endangered Species Act protections unchanged, because a bill with no cosponsors never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Delta fish and the salmon fishing economy

for.name: Rep. Jim Costa
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to loosen Endangered Species Act pumping limits on the Central Valley and State Water Projects.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so it never drew a party-line fight; it simply lacked the support to move [S4].

industries.industry: Central Valley agricultural water contractors (irrigation districts and large growers)
industries.note: Had it passed, they would have received fuller water deliveries by lifting the flow and pumping restrictions in the 2008 and 2009 biological opinions. The bill's own findings link those restrictions to fallowed land and high unemployment in valley farm towns, so some benefit reaches farmworkers, but the deliveries and the water rights go to the contractors.
Weakened Old and Middle River flow limits and expanded spring pumping would have increased the risk to salmon runs that support ocean and river fishing jobs in California and Oregon.

industries.industry: California freshwater fishing and delta communities
industries.note: Relaxed salinity standards and preemption of stricter state rules would have left the delta estuary and its recreation economy with fewer enforceable protections.
